blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A parcel job opens a new H2 connection, queues five INSERTs on one PreparedStatement with addBatch(), and calls executeBatch(). The fourth row has a NULL weight for a NOT NULL column, and the job catches the BatchUpdateException and exits without any other JDBC call. How many of the five rows does another session then count in the table?

options.text: None, since the batch reached the database in one call and the driver undid it as one unit.
options.says: One call into the driver is not one transaction: under auto-commit each statement of the batch committed on its own.

options.text: None, since a batch opens a transaction that stays pending until the job calls commit().
options.says: A new connection is in auto-commit mode, and a batch doesn't change that; the rows were committed as they ran.

options.text: Four, since the driver ran on past the failed row and each row was committed as it ran.
options.says: The page's batch under auto-commit returned [1, 1, -3, 1] and kept rows a, b and d: H2 continued after the failed row and auto-commit, on by default, committed each statement.

options.text: Three, since the driver stops at the first failed row and keeps the rows it ran before it.
options.says: The javadoc lets a driver stop at the first failure, but H2 doesn't: on the page it ran the row after the failed one and kept it.

origin.section: Auto-Commit Is On, So Each Statement Commits by Itself

questions.stem: A store report keeps one PreparedStatement, byRegion. It is looping over the stores of region N when it sets the parameter to S and calls byRegion.executeQuery() to look up a neighbouring store, then goes back to the loop. What does the loop's next call to next() do?

options.text: It returns the next store in N, since byRegion copied the N rows into memory.
options.says: Where the driver keeps the rows doesn't matter: a result set belongs to its statement, and re-executing the statement closed it.

options.text: It returns the next store in N, since the N cursor stays open with the connection.
options.says: Closing or re-executing the statement closes its result set, while the connection is still open.

options.text: It throws, since byRegion rejected the query for S and the N cursor broke with it.
options.says: A PreparedStatement is parsed once and executed many times, with new values bound each time; the second query ran fine.

options.text: It throws, since the query for S closed the N cursor that byRegion had opened.
options.says: The ResultSet javadoc says a result set closes when its statement is re-executed; the page's run printed isClosed() = true for the first one.

origin.section: A ResultSet Lives Only as Long as Its Statement

questions.stem: A clinic stores appointments in a TIMESTAMP column, and one row holds 2025-03-30 02:15:00. Server A runs with -Duser.timezone=UTC, server B with Europe/Paris, where clocks went from 02:00 to 03:00 that night. Both read the value with rs.getTimestamp(i).toLocalDateTime(). What do they show?

options.text: Both show 02:15, since a zoneless column is passed through unchanged on either server.
options.says: That is what getObject(i, LocalDateTime.class) does; getTimestamp builds an instant first, and the page's Berlin run showed 03:30.

options.text: Both show 03:15, since the database moved the time in the gap forward when it stored it.
options.says: The stored value is unchanged: getObject(i, LocalDateTime.class) read 02:30 on the page, and the UTC run read 02:30 with getTimestamp too.

options.text: A shows 02:15 and B throws, since B's zone has no 02:15 to build an instant from.
options.says: Nothing threw on the page: the time in the gap was moved forward an hour, silently.

options.text: A shows 02:15 and B shows 03:15, since each server builds an instant in its own zone.
options.says: getTimestamp reads the zoneless value in the JVM's default zone; 02:30 in Berlin's gap came back as 03:30 on the page, and with UTC it stayed 02:30.

origin.section: A Getter Converts; Ask getObject for the Java Type You Mean

questions.stem: A discount_pct INT column is NULL for customers who never had a discount and 0 for those whose discount was withdrawn. The code reads it with int pct = rs.getInt("discount_pct"). What does it get for each kind of customer?

options.text: 0 for both, since H2 stores SQL NULL in an INT column as the value 0.
options.says: The NULL is stored: getObject(i, Integer.class) returned null for the same row on the page.

options.text: 0 for both, since getInt turns SQL NULL into 0 when it reads the column.
options.says: The page's run printed getInt 0 for the NULL row and the 0 row alike; only wasNull() right after, or getObject(3, Integer.class), which returned null, tells them apart.

options.text: An SQLException for the NULL rows, since getInt can't put SQL NULL in an int.
options.says: getInt doesn't throw on NULL; it returns 0, which is why wasNull() exists.

options.text: A NullPointerException for the NULL rows, since getInt unboxes a null Integer.
options.says: getInt returned 0 for the NULL row on the page, and nothing threw.

origin.section: A Getter Converts; Ask getObject for the Java Type You Mean

concepts: A new connection is in auto-commit mode, so each statement commits on its own and a failure after the first leaves it committed; a batch is no exception.
getInt returns 0 for SQL NULL; wasNull() or getObject(i, Integer.class) tells NULL from 0.
A ResultSet is closed when its statement is closed or executed again, so rows are read into objects before the statement closes.
getTimestamp reads a zoneless TIMESTAMP through the JVM's default zone and moves a time in a DST gap; getObject(i, LocalDateTime.class) returns the stored value.
